prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth strip places the camera wearer’s forearm/hand and the large slanted panel within roughly 0.2–0.8 m, with the bucket/container around 0.7–1.2 m and the ground/background extending about 1–3+ m away; these estimates are approximate because monocular depth has no reliable metric scale. Across frames 1–4, the panel stays immediately in front and slightly right while its bright near edge shifts left/right with the wearer’s viewpoint, revealing its separation from the darker, farther ground more clearly than RGB alone. In frame 5, another person appears on the right at roughly 0.5–1.2 m, partly outside the image, with their nearer arm/hand overlapping the work area and the wearer’s foreground arm. Depth discontinuities around hands, the panel edge, bucket, and frame boundaries look smeared or inconsistent, so fine separations, person-facing direction, eye contact, and exact distances between people cannot be trusted.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map isolates a knife-like object in frame 1, left/front of the wearer and apparently within arm’s reach at roughly 0.3–0.8 m, even though its boundary and identity are less distinct in the RGB view. It detects no clear instances in frames 2–3, then marks a person on the right in frame 4 and a larger, partly out-of-view person on the far right in frame 5; the latter is close enough to overlap the foreground workspace, roughly 0.5–1.5 m from the wearer. The masks show that these people are right of the panel and partly occluded or cropped, but they do not encode depth, facing direction, gaze, or reliable distances from the knife or wearer. The map is unreliable spatially because many obvious objects—including the panel, bucket, arms, ground items, and most of the knife after frame 1—are missing, while the frame-4 person mask is fragmented and some labels are clipped.
descriptions.pose: The pose map is entirely black across all five frames, so it supplies no body or hand landmarks and supports no estimate of posture, facing direction, gaze, reach, or interpersonal separation. It also cannot distinguish the camera wearer’s visible foreground arm from the other person appearing at the right in frames 4–5, nor track approach, retreat, or turning over time. Relative scene layout must therefore come from the RGB, depth, and segmentation strips; for this sequence the pose output appears to be a failed or absent detection rather than evidence that no people or hands are present.
